groups.title: Password Security
groups.question: Explain how you would store user passwords safely in your API, and why each step matters.

followUps.bcrypt & Adaptive Hashing: Why is a fast hash like SHA-256 a bad choice for passwords, and what does bcrypt's cost factor do?
followUps.Salt — Why Random Salts Matter: Two users pick the same password. What makes their stored hashes different, and what attack does that stop?

evidence.text: A fast hash lets an attacker with stolen hashes try billions of guesses per second.
bcrypt is deliberately slow, and its cost factor sets how slow.
The cost factor can be raised over time as hardware gets faster.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (bcrypt, hashing, SHA-256) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says passwords should be encrypted so they can be decrypted later.

evidence.text: A random salt per password makes the same password produce different hashes.
That defeats precomputed rainbow tables and hides which users share a password.
The salt isn't secret; it is stored alongside the hash, and bcrypt handles it automatically.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (salt, rainbow table) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the salt must be kept secret, or that one fixed salt for all users is fine.

groups.title: JWT Authentication
groups.question: Walk through how JWT authentication works in an API, from login to a protected request, including how sessions end.

followUps.JWT Structure, Signing & the 'alg:none': Which part of a JWT actually provides security, and why should the server never trust the algorithm named in the token header?
followUps.Refresh Token Rotation & Token Revocatio: A refresh token gets stolen. How do rotation and a revocation list limit the damage?

evidence.text: A JWT has a header, a payload and a signature; header and payload are only encoded, not encrypted.
Only the signature, checked with the server's key, proves the token wasn't forged or changed.
The server must enforce its own algorithm, because the attacker controls the header and could claim none or a weaker one.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (JWT, signature, alg:none) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the payload is encrypted, so secrets can be stored in it.

evidence.text: Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens live longer and are used to get new access tokens.
Rotation issues a new refresh token on each use and invalidates the old one, so a reused stolen token is detected.
A revocation list, for example in Redis, lets you kill tokens at logout or after theft, before they expire.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (refresh token, rotation, revocation) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says deleting the token on the client revokes it.

groups.title: OAuth 2.0
groups.question: Explain how OAuth 2.0 lets one app access another service, and how you pick the right flow.

followUps.OAuth 2.0 Flows — Authorization Code vs: When would you use client credentials instead of the authorization code flow, and why is it unsafe in a browser app?
followUps.PKCE — Securing the Authorization Code F: A mobile app can't keep a client secret. What does PKCE add so an intercepted authorization code is useless?

evidence.text: The authorization code flow is for a user granting an app access, through a login and consent redirect.
Client credentials is for server-to-server calls with no user involved.
Client credentials needs a secret, and anything in a browser app's code can be read by any user.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (OAuth, authorization code, client credentials) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says OAuth works by giving the user's password to the other app.

evidence.text: The app makes a random secret (the code verifier) and sends only its hash (the challenge) with the authorization request.
To swap the code for tokens it must present the original verifier.
So someone who intercepts the code can't use it without the verifier.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (PKCE, code verifier) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says PKCE encrypts the authorization code.

groups.title: API Hardening
groups.question: Explain what you would configure to protect an API that a browser frontend calls, beyond authentication.

followUps.CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: What does CORS protect against, and what goes wrong if you allow any origin while also allowing credentials?
followUps.helmet.js & Security Headers: Name a security header that helmet.js sets and the attack it blocks.

evidence.text: Browsers block a page from reading responses from another origin unless the server allows that origin.
It stops other websites from using a visitor's cookies or credentials to read your API's responses.
Reflecting any origin while allowing credentials lets any site act as the logged-in user, so use an explicit allowlist.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (CORS, origin, preflight) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says CORS protects the API from non-browser clients like curl or other servers.

evidence.text: Names a header and the attack it stops, e.g. X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors against clickjacking, nosniff against MIME sniffing, HSTS against downgrade to HTTP, CSP against injected scripts.
These headers tell the browser how to treat the response defensively.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (helmet, security headers) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says helmet encrypts responses or replaces authentication.
